We measure energy access progress in kilowatt-hours, but the real question is: kilowatt-hours for what?
 
Energy is now at the centre of economic resilience and national security. In recent weeks alone, oil prices have surged by up to 50 percent. At the same time, clean cooking remains the furthest behind, affecting over 2 billion people and closely linked to health, gender, and air quality outcomes.
 
As we move closer to 2030, the challenge is no longer ambition, but delivery, scale, and impact.
 
This was the focus of today’s discussions at the #SDG7 Expert Group Meeting in Geneva, where I moderated Interactive Discussion 1: “Mobilizing a Final Push Towards SDG7.” The meeting was convened by UNDESA and hosted by UNECE Sustainable Energy in preparation for the 2026 SDG7 review at the High-Level Political Forum.
 
Three priorities stood out for the final push toward SDG7.
 
🔹 First, unlocking private sector capital at scale. Up to 90% of financing across energy systems will need to come from international private capital in most countries. The constraint is not the volume of finance, but its cost and risk. We need to move beyond funding toward financial architecture by scaling blended finance, guarantees, and risk-sharing mechanisms.
🔹 Second, strengthening policy coherence and governance for energy security and resilience. Energy poverty is increasingly concentrated in fragile and conflict-affected settings. 13 of 18 countries with the largest access deficits are affected by conflict. Progress depends not only on infrastructure, but on strong national systems, including local financial ecosystems, institutional capacity, maintenance, and skills that can enable the diversification of energy systems toward clean, affordable, and accessible energy.
🔹 Third, acting as one UN system to integrate energy into national development strategies and deliver on country priorities. 2 in 3 health facilities in low- and middle-income countries still lack reliable energy. Energy is deeply interconnected with agriculture, health, industry, and livelihoods, making it the operational backbone of the development. This creates an opportunity to advance integrated systems that align access, affordability, and productive use to deliver greater impact.
 
If we act as a system and align policy, finance, and delivery, we can turn the energy transition into the largest development opportunity of this decade.
 
This means focusing on impact: cleaner air, better health, gender equality, economic opportunity, and reaching 1.18 billion people who live in energy poverty, lacking adequate, reliable, and affordable energy for essential daily activities.
 
This is why the SDG7 review at the 2026 High-Level Political Forum will be such a critical moment for global development.
 
Looking forward to continuing these conversations and working with partners to deliver the final push toward SDG7.
